summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang; Tianzuo Li; Jiyeon Lee; Dahye Lim; Lianjie Xu; Yajie Liu; Jongcheol Seo; Wen-Bin Zhang

Executive Summary
This study reports the design and synthesis of cat-DHFR, a single-domain protein catenane derived from Escherichia coli dihydrofolate reductase. Unlike previous topological proteins requiring multiple domains or exogenous templates, cat-DHFR consists of two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings formed by rewiring the connectivity of the wild-type DHFR secondary motifs. The synthesis was achieved in E. coli using mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs, eliminating the need for in vitro reactions. Characterization via LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, and ion mobility mass spectrometry confirmed the catenane topology. While cat-DHFR exhibits reduced catalytic activity compared to the linear control due to compromised substrate affinity, it demonstrates enhanced stability against thermal and chemical denaturation. This work establishes that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated counterparts with identical chemical composition, preserved function, and elevated stability, opening new horizons in protein science.

Research Context
Natural protein domains are based on linear polypeptide chains. Natural protein domains have quite limited topological diversity. Discovery of natural topological proteins suggests enhanced stability. Artificial topological proteins usually contain multiple domains. Multiple domains complicate the study of topological effects. A single-domain topological protein shall exhibit the most profound impact. It remains challenging to prepare such single-domain topological proteins.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to convert a model enzyme into its single-domain catenane counterpart. The hypothesis is that rewiring loop regions can introduce artificial entanglement. Using the original fold as a template may eliminate the need for exogenous motifs. The hypothesis predicts that cat-DHFR will retain catalytic capability. The hypothesis predicts enhanced stability against denaturation due to conformational restriction. The design assumes that high Gaussian linking number indicates potential entanglement. The hypothesis predicts that circular permutation causes minor local disturbance.

Methodological Details
The target molecule contains few exogenous motifs. Synthesis was accomplished by programmed streamlined post-translational processing. The study used DHFR from Escherichia coli as the model enzyme. The design utilized a cleavage site between residues 88 and 89. The design generated two highly intertwined segments with a GLN of +0.726. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24. The rewired loops were designed to be long enough (16 residues). Expression was carried out in E.coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. Protein expression was carried out at 16 o C for 20 h. Purification used Ni-NTA affinity chromatography followed by size exclusion chromatography. The linear control (l-DHFR) bears extra amino acids not present in the wild-type. Topology proof utilized a TEV protease recognition sequence in the first ring. Characterization included LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry.

Procedures And Architectures
The design rewires connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement. The gene cassette contained two DHFR segments as the entangling template. The cassette included two mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs for ring closure. The cassette included the tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease recognition sequence. The split-intein pairs facilitate a streamlined synthesis of protein heterocatenanes. Circular permutation was necessary to place cyclization motifs on the opposite side. The method requires extensive optimization to achieve high-yield expression. Steric hindrance of bulky split-intein pairs affects reconstitution efficiency. The linker length plays an important role in reconstitution. Shorter linkers lead to a decrease in the yield of catenane. The yield with the shortest linker is only about one-fifth that of the longest. Crystallography attempts failed to obtain crystals of sufficient quality. Topology was confirmed by proteolytic digestion converting cat-DHFR to linear and cyclic fragments. Advanced mass spectrometry techniques included ion mobility spectrometry and collision-induced dissociation.

Key Results
SDS-PAGE analysis showed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR. cat-DHFR showed a major band at less than 20 kDa. cat-DHFR elutes as a much broader peak at a slightly larger retention volume. LC-MS spectra confirmed the accurate molecular weights of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Far-UV CD spectra showed reduced intensities of peaks for cat-DHFR. Near-UV CD spectrum exhibited a positive ellipticity at ~290 nm similar to the linear control. cat-DHFR has a lower activity (~5 U/mg) than the linear control (~14 U/mg). The Km of cat-DHFR is approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR. The kcat of cat-DHFR is about 38% that of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency of cat-DHFR is reduced by an order of magnitude. The dissociation constant for DHF is ~173-fold larger for cat-DHFR. The dissociation constant for NADPH is ~14-fold larger for cat-DHFR. cat-DHFR preserved 87% activity in 5% DMSO compared to 74% for l-DHFR. The KD between cat-DHFR and the product THF is increased by ~3.6-fold.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results suggest linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts. The counterparts have almost identical chemical composition. The counterparts have well-preserved function. The counterparts have elevated stability. This represents an entirely new horizon in protein science. Mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal resilience of the enzyme. The reduced activity is mainly attributed to compromised affinity towards substrate and cofactor. The binding of NADPH significantly enhances the affinity of cat-DHFR towards DHF. The product can also easily leave the enzyme due to increased KD. Directed evolution may further restore the activity to match the linear control.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study failed to obtain crystals of sufficient quality for unambiguous proof of topology. Crystallography failure may be due to unsatisfactory purity or disordered linkers. cat-DHFR exhibits substantially reduced intensities in far-UV CD spectra. This suggests a loosening of the secondary structure compared to the linear control. Circular permutation may cause minor local disturbance on local folded structures. The yield with the shortest linker is significantly lower than the longest. The method is generally robust before the linker becomes too short.

Data And Code Availability
Sequence information is available in the Supporting Information.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The construct using split-intein ligation pairs on the same side formed much less catenane. Circular permutation was necessary to place cyclization motifs on the opposite side. The site between residues 23 and 24 was found to be the most efficient one. Shorter linkers lead to a decrease in the yield of catenane.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the design of cat-DHFR with residues 1-88 and 89-159. Figure 2a shows SDS-PAGE analysis of purified products. Figure 2b shows SEC overlay of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Figure 2c shows LC-MS spectra confirming molecular weights. Figure 2d shows far-UV CD spectra of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Figure 4c shows kinetic curves of DHFR samples. Table 1 lists kinetic parameters Km and kcat.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of DHFR. 2. The strongest evidence is the retention of catalytic capability and enhanced stability. 3. The future path involves directed evolution to restore activity and further engineering.
